properties.name: Colchester
properties.one_line: Britannia's first provincial temple, dedicated to the deified Claudius soon after the conquest, was the grandest building in the new colonia. Boudica's rebels burned it to its podium in 60 CE, trapping the last defenders inside for two days before the walls fell. Rome rebuilt the temple on the same massive podium, which still underlies Colchester Castle today.

properties.name: Tarragona
properties.one_line: The provincial council of Hispania Citerior petitioned Rome for a temple to the deified Augustus, and Tacitus later called the grant the precedent every other province followed. Dedicated under Tiberius around 15 CE, it stood at the center of a 7.5-hectare forum complex crowning Tarraco's acropolis and hosted the province's annual assembly. Hadrian would rebuild the temple in 123 CE, but in 117 it was already a century into continuous use.
properties.image_credit: Les Ferreres Aqueduct, Tarraco (Tarragona) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Pergamon
properties.one_line: Pergamon became the first city in Asia Minor allowed a temple to a living emperor when Augustus granted the province's request in 29 BCE. The temple to Roma and Augustus crowned the acropolis beside the older sanctuary of Athena and made Pergamon the political and religious capital of the koinon of Asia. Trajan added a second temple on the same acropolis, still unfinished at his death in 117 CE and completed by Hadrian.
properties.image_credit: The Hellenistic Theatre of Pergamon · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Izmit
properties.one_line: Nicomedia earned the same honor as Pergamon in the same year, 29 BCE, when Augustus authorized a temple to Roma and the deified Julius Caesar for the province's Roman-citizen population. It served for decades as a meeting place of Bithynia's provincial assembly, alongside Pergamon's temple for Asia. Modern Izmit sits directly over the ancient city, and the temple itself has never been relocated archaeologically.
properties.image_credit: Roman aqueduct of Nicomedia, Izmit · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.first_worshipped: Domitian and Domitia (now venerated as Divus Vespasianus)
properties.one_line: Dedicated in 89-90 CE, this temple made Ephesus the first city in the province to hold the title neokoros, temple-warden of an emperor, under a colossal cult statue that stood well over 6 meters tall. After Domitian's assassination and damnatio memoriae in 96 CE, the sanctuary was quietly rededicated to his deified father Vespasian rather than torn down. In 117 CE it still closed the south side of Domitian Square between the State Agora and Curetes Street.
properties.image_credit: Nymphaeum of Trajan, Ephesus · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ankara
properties.one_line: Built soon after Rome annexed Galatia in 25 BCE, this temple to Roma and Augustus carries the most complete surviving copy of the Res Gestae Divi Augusti, Augustus's own account of his career, cut into its interior walls in Latin with a Greek translation running along the exterior. Scholars still call it the Monumentum Ancyranum for that inscription. The text remained legible on the temple walls in 117 CE, more than a century after it was carved.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The Temple of Augustus and Rome with the Res Gestae Divi Augusti ("Deeds of the Divine Augustus") inscribed on the walls of the cella, Ancyra, Ankara (Turkey) (25821691100).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Temple of Augustus and Rome, Ancyra (Ankara) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Aphrodisias
properties.first_worshipped: Augustus, Tiberius, Claudius and Nero (the Julio-Claudian dynasty)
properties.one_line: Local families funded this three-story processional complex across three generations, lining its two 90-meter porticoes with more than 190 carved relief panels celebrating the Julio-Claudian emperors as conquerors and gods. Completed under Nero around 60 CE, it linked a monumental gate to a temple of Aphrodite at its western end. The reliefs and colonnades still stood complete in 117 CE.

properties.name: Pisidian Antioch
properties.one_line: A triple-arched gateway opened onto this hillside sanctuary, its temple to Augustus set on a high podium and framed by a two-story colonnaded courtyard cut into the slope. The propylon carried a Latin copy of the Res Gestae Divi Augusti, one of only three copies of the text known from the ancient world. Roman veteran colonists settled here by Augustus kept the sanctuary in continuous use through 117 CE.

properties.name: Narbonne
properties.first_worshipped: Numen Augusti (the divine power of the living Augustus)
properties.one_line: The people of Narbo vowed this altar to the numen of Augustus in 11 CE, five years after Rome itself set up an altar to the same cult, and dedicated it the following year in the city's forum. Its inscribed rules for sacrifice survive nearly complete, laying out an annual calendar of offerings on Augustus's birthday and accession day. Narbo, capital of the senatorial province Gallia Narbonensis, kept the cult running through 117 CE, separate from the federal altar the three Gauls shared at Lugdunum.

properties.name: Veria
properties.one_line: Beroea hosted the koinon of Macedonians, the province's federal council, and its Sebasteion made the city Macedonia's religious center of emperor worship. Nerva granted Beroea the coveted neokoros title only two decades before this snapshot, a fresh honor Macedonians were still celebrating in 117 CE. A Macedoniarch presided each year over the games and sacrifices held there.

properties.name: Carthage
properties.one_line: A freedman named Perelius Hedulus, serving as Carthage's lifetime priest of the imperial cult, dedicated this marble altar to the Gens Augusta on the slopes of Byrsa hill, inside the colony Caesar and Augustus had refounded on Carthage's ruins in 29 BCE. Its carved reliefs of Roma and Apollo echoed the Ara Pacis back in Rome. As capital of Africa Proconsularis, Carthage remained the province's foremost center of emperor worship when Trajan died in 117 CE.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Roman amphitheatre of Carthage - inner view south.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Roman amphitheatre of Carthage · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Cordoba
properties.one_line: Corduba, capital of Hispania Baetica, raised this Corinthian temple on a terraced platform beside its provincial forum, a project begun under Claudius that took roughly forty years to finish under Domitian. Six columns crossed its front and ten ran down each side, making it one of the largest temples ever built in Roman Spain. It hosted Baetica's annual provincial assembly and imperial cult through 117 CE.
properties.image_credit: Roman Temple of Calle Claudio Marcelo, Corduba (Cordoba) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Alexandria
properties.first_worshipped: Divus Julius Caesar, completed as a temple of Augustus
properties.one_line: Cleopatra began this harborside sanctuary to honor Mark Antony or Julius Caesar; after her defeat at Actium, Augustus finished it instead as his own temple of the imperial cult. Twin obelisks over 20 meters tall, dragged from Heliopolis, flanked its entrance and were later carried off to London and New York as Cleopatra's Needles. Philo of Alexandria, writing within a generation of 117 CE, called it unmatched anywhere in the world for its size and beauty.
properties.image_credit: The Caesareum of Alexandria, seat of the imperial cult · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Caesarea
properties.one_line: Herod the Great built this temple on a raised platform overlooking the artificial harbor he had just engineered, dedicating it jointly to the goddess Roma and to Augustus around 10 BCE. Visible far out at sea, it announced Caesarea as a thoroughly Roman city before a ship ever reached the breakwater. Caesarea had served as the seat of Judaea's Roman governors for more than a century by 117 CE, and the temple still crowned the city center.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Temple of Roma and Augustus (Caesarea Maritima) DSC05221.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Temple of Roma and Augustus, Caesarea Maritima · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Sebastia
properties.one_line: Herod the Great rebuilt the old Israelite capital of Samaria, renamed it Sebaste, Greek for Augustus, and crowned its acropolis with a temple to his patron measuring roughly 35 by 24 meters. The temple sat directly over the ruins of the biblical kings' palace complex on the hilltop. It remained the ceremonial center of Herodian loyalty to Rome through 117 CE, a debt written into the very name of the city.

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Tiberius and Livia built this temple over the house where Augustus had lived before entering public life, establishing Rome's own cult of its first deified emperor. Caligula finished the dedication and, according to Suetonius, used its roof as a bridge to visit the Capitoline as though he were the god's equal. Domitian rebuilt the temple after a fire around 89-90 CE, and it stood between the Palatine and Capitoline hills in full cult use in 117 CE.

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Titus began this temple for his deified father Vespasian in 79 CE, and after Titus himself died and was deified the next year, Domitian rededicated it to both of them jointly around 87 CE. Three of its Corinthian columns still stand today at over 15 meters tall. It closed the western end of the Roman Forum between the Temple of Concord and the Temple of Saturn, in active cult use in 117 CE.

properties.name: Rome
properties.one_line: Agrippina began this temple on the Caelian Hill for her poisoned and deified husband Claudius in 54 CE, raising a podium roughly 180 by 200 meters, one of the largest temple platforms in Rome. Her son Nero abandoned the project and carved a monumental nymphaeum into its unfinished eastern wall instead. Vespasian finally completed the temple decades later, and it stood finished and in cult use in 117 CE.

properties.name: Pula
properties.one_line: Pula's colonists raised this temple to Roma and Augustus on the north edge of the forum between 2 BCE and 14 CE, the eastern member of a row of three. It stands 14 metres tall on its podium behind four Corinthian columns, its frieze carved with vines and birds. An Allied bomb flattened it in 1944 and masons rebuilt it stone by stone from the rubble. By 117 it had already stood a century.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Templo de Augusto, Pula, Croacia, 2017-04-17, DD 71-73 HDR.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Diego Delso, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

properties.name: Vienne
properties.one_line: Vienne raised this temple to Roma and Augustus at the head of its forum under Augustus, then rebuilt it around 40 CE and cut Livia's name into the architrave beside her husband's. Six Corinthian columns carry the front, and the temple still stands to its full height, one of only two in France that do. It served as a church, then a courthouse, then a museum. In 117 it was well over a century old.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Temple of Augustus and Livia, Vienne, France (9039439703).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

properties.name: Nimes
properties.one_line: Nemausus dedicated this temple to Gaius and Lucius Caesar, Augustus's grandsons and chosen heirs, both dead before the work finished around 5 CE. Thirty engaged Corinthian columns ring the walls. Medieval hands stripped the bronze dedication letters, but in 1758 a local scholar read the text back off the nail holes left in the frieze. It has never lost its roof in twenty centuries.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Merida
properties.one_line: Emerita Augusta set this temple on the east side of its civic forum in the first years of the empire and gave it to the emperor's cult, not to Diana, whose name a later antiquarian pinned on it by mistake. Six granite columns front the podium and the flanks are ringed by more. A Renaissance palace was built inside the cella and is still standing there. Lusitania's capital worshipped here for three centuries.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

properties.name: Athens
properties.one_line: The Athenian people set a round temple of nine Ionic columns on the Acropolis around 19 BCE, 23 metres due east of the Parthenon and aligned exactly with its front door. The architrave inscription names the goddess Roma and Augustus Caesar Soter, along with the priest and the archon of the year. Only foundations and scattered blocks survive. For a century and a half it held the emperor's image in Greece's most sacred sightline.
sources: IG II3 4, 10 (= IG II2 3173), architrave dedication of the temple of Roma and Augustus
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Remains of the Temple of Rome and Augustus (Athens) on 16 April 2018.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

properties.name: Iznik
properties.one_line: Augustus split emperor worship in Asia Minor in two in 29 BCE: Greek communities got the living ruler, Roman citizens got the dead one. Nicaea received the precinct of Roma and Divus Iulius for the citizens resident in Bithynia, the exact counterpart of Nicomedia's temple of Roma and Augustus. Cassius Dio records both grants in the same passage. The precinct has never been found under modern Iznik.
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The Roman Theatre of Nicaea built during the reign of Trajan, Iznik, Turkey (37742971275).jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Roman theatre of Nicaea, built under Trajan · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Izmir
properties.one_line: Eleven cities of Asia sent embassies to the Senate in 26 CE to compete for the province's second imperial temple, and Smyrna took it. The temple honoured Tiberius, his mother Livia and the Roman Senate together, making the Senate itself an object of worship. Tacitus reports the whole debate and the verdict. Smyrna held the title of temple warden from that day, and still held it in 117.
properties.image_credit: Agora of Smyrna · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Leptis Magna
properties.one_line: Leptis Magna began this temple to Roma and Augustus around 8 BCE and finished it between 14 and 19 CE, before the city was even a municipium. It measures roughly 46 by 20 metres and fills the north end of the Old Forum, and the whole community paid for it rather than one rich donor. Colossal statues of the imperial family stood inside. Second-century restorers replaced its limestone with marble.
sources: IPT 22, the Neo-Punic and Latin dedication of the temple of Augustus and Roma
properties.image_credit: Theatre of Leptis Magna · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Thessaloniki
properties.one_line: Thessalonica built a temple of Caesar under Augustus and staffed it with a priest of Imperator Caesar Augustus, son of god, recorded on a city inscription beside the older priest of the gods. Its mint dropped the local magistrates from the coinage and put Julius Caesar's head on the obverse instead. The building has never been located under the modern city. The cult was over a century old by 117.
sources: IG X 2.1 31, decree mentioning the temple of Caesar and the priest of Imperator Caesar Augustus
properties.image_credit: Roman Forum of Thessalonica · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ostia Antica
properties.one_line: Tiberius added this temple of Roma and Augustus to the south side of Ostia's forum, facing the older Capitolium across the square so the emperor's cult looked Jupiter straight in the eye. A flamen Romae et Augusti held the priesthood for life. Foundations survive along with the marble rear pediment and a winged Victory that once crowned the roof, now displayed on site.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA (Victory statue from the Temple of Roma and Augustus, Ostia Antica)

properties.name: Pozzuoli
properties.one_line: Lucius Calpurnius, a rich local, paid for Puteoli's temple of Augustus out of his own pocket and cut his name across the architrave, where it can still be read. His architect rebuilt it on the podium of a temple of 194 BCE, in white marble blocks fitted without mortar. Six Corinthian columns front the cella. A cathedral swallowed the temple in the sixth century, and a fire in 1964 burned the church back off it.
sources: Dedicatory architrave inscription: L. Calpurnius L. f. templum Augusto cum ornamentis d(e) s(ua) p(ecunia) f(ecit)
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

properties.name: Cyrene
properties.one_line: Cyrene converted a gymnasium of the 2nd century BCE into a Caesareum in Augustus's later years, enclosing a colonnaded court with a free-standing temple at its centre and two Doric gateways opening off the main streets. Ranks of its columns still stand. The Jewish revolt of 115 to 117 wrecked the city so thoroughly that Hadrian had to fund a rebuilding programme in 118.
sources: Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites, s.v. Cyrene: https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus:text:1999.04.0006:entry%3Dcyrene
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA

properties.name: Glanum
properties.one_line: Two matching temples went up side by side in Glanum's forum around 20 BCE, sharing a single walled precinct and serving the imperial cult. Portrait heads of Augustus's female relatives, Octavia and Julia among them, came out of the ruins. Only the podium and a partly re-erected facade survive, the rest of the marble having gone into local walls. Glanum kept them until the town was abandoned in the third century.
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA (general view of the Glanum archaeological site)

properties.name: Teos
properties.one_line: Teos put a temple of Roma in its agora and reworked it for the emperor's cult under Augustus, a change its Greek inscriptions record. The building is small, 8 by 18 metres, with pronaos, cella and opisthodomos, and it faces southwest rather than the usual east. Excavation in 2020 found a six-by-twelve Corinthian colonnade, overturning what everyone had assumed about the order.

properties.name: Narona
properties.one_line: Narona built its Augusteum around 10 BCE and the governor Publius Cornelius Dolabella later rededicated it. Archaeologists digging under the village of Vid in 1995 and 1996 struck the temple floor and 17 over-lifesize marble statues of emperors and their families, toppled and beheaded where they stood. The series runs from Augustus to the Flavians, so the shrine was still taking in new emperors in the second century.
sources: E. Marin, 'The temple of the imperial cult (Augusteum) at Narona and its statues: interim report', Journal of Roman Archaeology 14 (2001) 81-112
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Roman temple Augustum in Narona, 1. cent., Vid, Metkovic, Croatia 2010.JPG?width=800
properties.image_credit: Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

properties.name: Barcelona
properties.one_line: A four-column temple to Augustus dominated the tiny colony of Barcino, sited deliberately at the highest point in town where the cardo and decumanus crossed. Four of its Corinthian columns still stand today, walled into a courtyard just off Barcelona's Gothic Quarter.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Augustus, Barcelona · Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0

properties.name: Tres Arae Sestianae
properties.one_line: Three open-air altars raised on the wild Atlantic headland at Cape Finisterre around 19 BCE by the legate Lucius Sestius, marking the western edge of the known world as newly Roman. No temple, no roof -- just stone altars facing the ocean where the sun was believed to set into the sea.

properties.name: Banias
properties.one_line: Herod the Great raised a white marble temple to Augustus here, at the mouth of the cave the locals held sacred to Pan, in thanks for Augustus handing him the Golan. Its exact footprint among the sanctuary's ruins is still argued over -- one candidate sits right against the cave mouth, another lies south at Khirbet Omrit.
properties.image_credit: Corinthian column, Omrit temple complex (candidate site for Herod's Augusteum) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Szombathely
properties.first_worshipped: the imperial family of Pannonia Superior
properties.one_line: Savaria was Pannonia Superior's oldest colony, and its Ara Augustorum was the province's central altar -- the one place a Pannonian priest offered sacrifice on behalf of every emperor at once. Claudius founded the town; by Trajan's day it had been the seat of the provincial cult for two generations.

properties.name: Gortyn
properties.one_line: A temple to the deified emperors stood inside the governor's own palace complex at Gortyn, the seat of Roman power over Crete and Cyrenaica together. An inscribed doorjamb is what nails the dedication down -- the rest of the Praetorium's marble floors and courtyards survive around it.
properties.image_credit: Praetorium complex, Gortyn, Crete (site of the imperial-cult shrine) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Corinth
properties.first_worshipped: Roma and Augustus, then the imperial family
properties.one_line: Corinth hosted the federal cult of the Achaean koinon -- the assembly of Greek cities that met here to honor Rome and its emperors collectively, decades before Paul preached in the same forum. Refounded by Julius Caesar as a colony after standing empty since 146 BCE, it became the natural seat for provincial loyalty in 117 CE Achaea.
properties.image_credit: Temple E, Ancient Corinth (identified with the imperial/Octavia cult) · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Solin
properties.one_line: Dalmatia's provincial capital built a Temple of Augustus into its forum while the emperor was still alive, one of the earliest such temples anywhere in the western provinces. Most of Salona's forum still lies buried under the modern town of Solin, unexcavated.
properties.image_credit: Amphitheatre of Salona, near Solin · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Philippi
properties.one_line: Veterans of Philippi's founding battle got their land grants from Augustus, and the colony paid him back with a temple facing the forum's curia, holding statues of Caesar, Augustus and Livia together. Paul preached in this same forum a century after it was built.
properties.image_credit: The Forum of Philippi, where the imperial-cult temple stood · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Nicopolis
properties.one_line: Augustus built his victory monument on the hill where he had camped before Actium, ringed with captured warship rams and dedicated to Apollo -- then, after his death, a dedicated wing for his own cult, the Aedes Augustalium, was added onto it. The whole complex looks out over the strait where the battle that made him sole ruler was fought.
properties.image_credit: Augustus's Actium victory monument, Nicopolis, to which the Aedes Augustalium wing was attached · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Segobriga
properties.one_line: A small inland town in the Meseta built its whole forum around 15 BCE as an imperial-cult showcase, and kept it running: inscriptions name at least ten priests who served the cult here over the following century. The forum's dynastic statue cycle put the emperor's family alongside the town's own leading citizens.
properties.image_credit: Cryptoporticus of the Forum, Segobriga, Saelices · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Nola
properties.one_line: Augustus died in the house his father had died in, at Nola, on 19 August 14 CE -- and the Senate voted a temple for the very spot. Tiberius and Livia (ancient sources disagree which) finished it by 26 CE, making Nola one of the first places anywhere to house a cult of the newly deified first emperor.
